source.title: Are Protein Language Models Compute Optimal?
source.authors: Yaiza Serrano; Álvaro Ciudad; Alexis Molina

record.tranche_reason: The study adapts NLP scaling-law methods to protein language models and reports that its fitted losses are largely insensitive to parameter and token counts, with a common loss plateau. It also fits compute-optimal parameter and token trends, while arguing that NLP scaling laws may not transfer to pLMs.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own training-loss fits and compute-allocation estimates. Comparisons to RITA, ProteinBERT, xTrimoPGLM, ESM-2, and Frey et al. are reported from other works and are not recorded as this study's results. The 35M model's own held-out perplexity is recorded under fits_no_version: it is a single-model held-out result, not a scaling or downstream-prediction test.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own protein-model training-loss scaling and compute-allocation fits, and argues that NLP scaling laws do not transfer to its single-pass protein-model setting. These results bear on V3 and V5; they do not measure held-out-loss scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that NLP scaling laws are not transferable to pLMs, based on a shared training-loss plateau, and propose reaching that plateau efficiently as the training objective. They suggest larger models may reach it with fewer FLOPs and report competitive held-out perplexity for one 35M model. Their broad transfer conclusion exceeds their tested single-pass setting.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. scaling-law methodology to encoder-only protein language models trained with masked language modeling. It uses single-pass training and its own smoothing, interpolation, and plateau-based analyses; it is not a direct reproduction of either NLP study.
record.method_sensitivity: The study compares token-based learning-rate decay with no decay and reports the same plateau. It also uses different fitting approaches: combined parametric loss, linear regression, and polynomial fitting.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger tested models reportedly require fewer FLOPs to reach common training-loss thresholds, with negative fitted slopes at all three thresholds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger encoder-only protein models can reach a fixed training-loss plateau more compute-efficiently in this single-pass setup.

fits_no_version.finding: The 35M model achieves held-out perplexity 11.43 on the stated 8K-sequence evaluation set.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single-pass 35M protein model achieves the reported held-out perplexity under this evaluation protocol.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the ICML 2024 Workshop on Accessible and Efficient Foundation Models for Biological Discovery
record.problems: The key loss-scaling evidence is based on training loss and is not a held-out-loss scaling test. The reported critical values are described by the authors as unreasonable or extraordinarily large, and they state the fits were not informative about attaining lower loss. Several optimal model sizes are polynomial-fit estimates far beyond the tested model sizes, with no runs at those estimated sizes. No uncertainty estimates are reported. Downstream-task evaluation is left for future work.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible own-result rows identified. Literature comparisons to RITA, ProteinBERT, xTrimoPGLM, ESM-2 and Frey et al. are omitted because they are attributed to other works. The reported intercepts for the three linear regressions are not separate loss or allocation outcomes beyond the slopes captured in r9.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining-loss scaling across model sizes, token counts or compute; the scaling fits use training loss.
Validation of small-run predictions against actual runs orders of magnitude larger. The polynomial size estimates are not such validation.
Stability of the fitted allocation powers across compute ranges, and actual optimality at the extrapolated billion- and trillion-parameter sizes.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Held-out-loss scaling across protein models, repeated-data training, other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer.
Downstream-task scaling or prediction from pretraining loss; downstream evaluation is future work.

Comparative dependence of exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, parameter counting, datasets or schedules. Different fitting approaches address different quantities, and no schedule-specific exponent comparison is reported. A temporal convergence plateau alone does not establish bending of a scaling curve.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any version. The token range spans only about 3.2-fold, no fit uncertainty is reported, and the combined loss fit includes a negative critical dataset-size parameter. These constrain interpretation of the reported failure to transfer. Polynomial allocation estimates are retained as estimates, without treating them as measured optima.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits training loss, not held-out pretraining loss across parameters, tokens, or compute. Its single held-out perplexity result does not test a power-law relationship.
It does not validate predictions from power laws fitted on small runs against runs orders of magnitude larger.

Tests compute-allocation fits for encoder-only pLMs in the reported configurations, but does not establish that the trend remains stable beyond its tested range or compare the Kaplan and Hoffmann allocation exponents directly.
Model architectures vary to scale parameter count, but the study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Tests protein models and a single-pass training setup using training-loss fits. It does not test image or video models, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The reported held-out perplexity is not a downstream-task performance evaluation, and the authors state downstream evaluation is future work.

The study compares learning-rate-decay and no-decay training and uses power-law, linear, and polynomial fits. It does not systematically vary parameter-count conventions, datasets, or fitting procedures to establish why published laws disagree.

rows.subject: ESM-2 models (all tested configurations; 5M–650M)
rows.stage_stated: pretraining; masked language modeling; single epoch
rows.operation_detail: Fit the combined loss function to smoothed and interpolated final training losses across model sizes and dataset sizes.
rows.measure: Fitted loss-scaling parameters and authors' interpretation of sensitivity to model and dataset size
rows.value: αN = 0.0063; αD = 0.0074; Nc = 4.85 × 10^79; Dc = −1.33 × 10^69. Authors report minimal impact from increasing model and dataset size within the explored range.
rows.note: The authors describe the exponents as very small and the critical values as indicating that the fitted loss is relatively insensitive to N and D. This is a fit to training loss, not held-out loss.
rows.check: The authors describe loss improvements as minimal, and the negative fitted Dc makes the combined fit problematic. This is training-loss evidence against transfer in the tested range, not a comparison establishing V7 fitting dependence.

rows.operation_detail: Compare training-loss convergence plateaus across model configurations and learning-rate schedules.
rows.value: A common plateau at around 2.45; the text says the fitted models reached the same plateau regardless of learning-rate decay strategy.
rows.note: Aggregate finding across the reported configurations; values are training loss. The authors say the plateau was visible in both sets of training.
rows.check: The common training-loss plateau supports the reported absence of substantial scaling improvements. Its persistence under both schedules does not establish that scaling exponents or allocation depend on schedule.
